title: Shaping a boule
subtitle: The round sourdough loaf, how to build a tight skin and a strong seam
excerpt: Shaping a boule creates the surface tension that holds the loaf together during baking. The goal is a smooth, taut skin with a tight seam on the underside. Done right, the loaf holds its shape and springs upward in the oven rather than spreading sideways.
sourceNotes: Boule shaping technique follows standard sourdough bread-making practice. The method of pre-shaping, resting, and final shaping is established across contemporary home sourdough baking.

glossaryTerms.definition: A round sourdough loaf. The French word for ball. The shape is versatile and forgiving for home bakers because it does not require a tin.
The taut outer skin of a shaped loaf, created by pulling the dough smoothly over itself during shaping. Surface tension helps the loaf hold its form and spring upward during baking.
A brief, gentle round performed before the final shape. Pre-shaping redistributes the gas evenly and gives the dough a few minutes to relax before the final shaping.

After bulk fermentation, gently tip the dough onto an unfloured bench. Sprinkle flour lightly on top. Slide a bench scraper under the dough and fold the edges up and into the centre all the way around until it forms a loose round. Flip the dough seam-side down. Use the scraper and your free hand to drag the dough toward you along the bench, building light tension on the surface. Leave the
to rest uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes. The gluten relaxes and the final shape becomes easier.
Flip the pre-shaped round so the seam faces up. Gently flatten the dough slightly.
Fold the far edge of the dough in toward the centre. Then fold the left and right sides in. Finally fold the near edge up and over. The dough should look like an envelope.

Flip the round seam-side down. Cup your hands behind it and pull it toward you across the bench in short, sharp strokes. The skin should tighten with each drag. Stop when the surface is smooth and taut.

Dust a banneton generously with rice flour or a blend of rice and plain flour, plain flour alone tends to stick. Place the shaped boule seam-side up in the banneton. Fold the cloth over and refrigerate for the overnight proof. The cold retard firms the dough and makes scoring and loading into the oven much easier.
Work on an unfloured surface during final shaping. The slight drag of dough on the bench is what creates tension. A floured surface lets the dough slide without gripping.
